## Proof

Let
$$S = \{(a,b) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid a - b \in \mathbb{Q}\}.$$

For each $q \in \mathbb{Q}$, define the line
$$L_q = \{(a,b) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid a - b = q\}.$$

Then
$$S = \bigcup_{q \in \mathbb{Q}} L_q.$$

**Each $L_q$ has Lebesgue measure 0.** Indeed, $L_q$ is an affine line in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (a translate of the 1-dimensional subspace $\{(t,t) : t \in \mathbb{R}\}$). Any affine subspace of dimension $< 2$ has 2-dimensional Lebesgue measure $0$. Concretely, $L_q$ is contained in the strip $\{(a,b) : q-\varepsilon \le a-b \le q+\varepsilon\}$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$, which has measure $2\varepsilon \cdot \infty$... more cleanly: $L_q$ is the graph of $b = a - q$, and the graph of any measurable function has measure $0$ (cover by $\varepsilon$-tubes of measure $\le 2\varepsilon \cdot n$ on bounded regions, then exhaust $\mathbb{R}^2$).

**$\mathbb{Q}$ is countable**, so $S$ is a countable union of measure-zero sets. By countable subadditivity of Lebesgue measure,
$$m(S) \le \sum_{q \in \mathbb{Q}} m(L_q) = \sum_{q \in \mathbb{Q}} 0 = 0.$$

Since measure is nonnegative, $m(S) = 0$.
